articles.title: Pope’s visit to Argentina sets up showdown with ‘hyper-capitalist’ Milei
articles.summary:
President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’

Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are…

blocks.text: Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.

But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.

“[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”.

Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy.

The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024.

Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.”
Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.”

But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation.

Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.”

Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.”

Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse.

The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”.

All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself.

“I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel.

Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.”

Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.”
To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.”

That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”.

But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.

Nevertheless, a majority of Argentines expect a “message from the pope focused on the social and humanitarian agenda”. Grabois notes the transformative impact that first Francis and now Leo have had “with left-leaning activists” in Argentina. “I’m not speaking about atheists, but outright anticlerical people. People who, 10 years ago, held views that were very, very hostile toward the church,” he said. “I even see them as more fervent [about the visit] than typical churchgoers who attend Sunday Mass.” For Grabois, “in the face of dehumanisation, ordinary people are taking refuge in the only global voice that’s speaking out about this today – which is Francis and Leo’s.”

articles.title: Psychiatrists and paediatricians among specialists most likely to charge ‘extreme’ fees, thinktank finds
articles.summary:
Grattan Institute finds some doctors charge up to triple the fees of their peers – well beyond what can be justified by business running costs

  • Get our

blocks.text: More than 2.2 million Australians paid an “extreme” fee to see a specialist last year, with psychiatrists and paediatricians among the most likely to routinely unreasonably charge their patients, according to new research.

Specialists cannot justify exorbitant fees by blaming inadequate government rebates, or the costs of running a business, a report from policy thinktank the Grattan Institute found, as these factors explain only a fraction of the fee increases Australians have faced.

While Medicare rebates fell in real terms by $9 per between 2012 and 2025, specialists increased patient fees by an average of $37 over the same period, recouping the lost subsidy more than four times over. The average specialist fee rose 4% on top of inflation in 2025.

The report, Out of control – how to rein in runaway specialist fees, published on Sunday, defines an extreme fee as being at least triple the official Medicare schedule fee, which is the benchmark price set by the government.
Extreme fees are becoming more common, the report found, with 250,000 extra patients paying them each year, affecting 2.2 million patients in 2025.
“Some specialists routinely charge patients much more than their peers,” the report found.
“The most expensive 5% of psychiatrists charge a median out-of-pocket fee of $669 for an initial consultation. For high-cost paediatricians, it is $362. For high-cost cardiologists, it is $265.11.”
These specialists charge 104%, 212% and 203% more than their peers, respectively.

Among several recommendations, the report calls on the government to force any specialist whose annual fees average more than three times the Medicare schedule fee to repay the government for all rebates claimed that year. Patients would keep their rebate.
This would affect roughly 6% of specialists nationwide (about 2,000 doctors), but more than 60% of private dermatologists and a quarter of obstetrician-gynaecologists.

The median fee for an initial consultation has also risen faster than inflation, with an initial dermatology consultation increasing by $28 to $217.8 between 2023 and 2025, the report found. For psychiatry, it rose by $90, reaching $351.

In 2025, fewer than a quarter of initial consultations were bulk-billed, and fewer than 10% of initial consultations in urology, dermatology, otolaryngology (ear, nose and throat), and psychiatry were bulk-billed.

The lead author of the report, health economist Peter Breadon, said increased price transparency was important but would not be enough to fix what he described as a broken market failing to self-regulate.

In September, legislation passed allowing the government to publish the fees of all specialists on the Medical Costs Finder website, which will commence in 2027. The website has been voluntary for specialists to sign up to, with only about 100 out of 6,300 eligible specialists publicly disclosing their fees since it was established in 2019.

“Some doctors, and some of their advocacy groups, have said self-regulation is the way forward, by appealing to people’s interest in making sure their patients can get the care they need,” Breadon said.

“That kind of approach isn’t working. This is a long-term trend and the real reason is it’s a market where none of the forces that would normally constrain fee growth are working. There’s very little competition because there are not enough specialists to go around, and there is a long public wait.
“It’s also very hard for patients to understand whether a fee is too high, because there is little information about how to evaluate the quality of care. It means regulation is the sensible step.”

The report calls on federal and state governments to invest $500m each year to expand public hospital outpatient clinics; to roll out advice lines for GPs to quickly seek specialist advice so their patients can avoid a referral, wait time and fees; and to impose binding training quotas on medical colleges.
Without reform, Breadon said: “This is not a system that’s going to self-correct.
“It’s been left to run on autopilot for decades.”

The CEO of the Consumers Health Forum, Dr Elizabeth Deveny, said Australians were increasingly “rationing their own care or skipping follow ups simply because the gap costs more than a week of groceries”.
“When the only alternative is a two year public waitlist, people pay because they have run out of options,” she said.
In response to the recommendations, the federal health minister, Mark Butler, told Guardian Australia “all options are on the table to rein in climbing specialist fees”.
The government has established a specialist affordability working group to advise on reforms, of which Breadon is a member.
The Royal College of Physicians president-elect, Dr Julian Kelly, said the peak body would support the government in introducing any regulation to address extreme charging.
“The RACP does not defend excessive fees that create barriers to care or place unreasonable financial pressure on patients,” Kelly said.

“Extreme fee charing is unacceptable. We acknowledge the Grattan Institute’s contribution to this important discussion and agree that improving affordability and access to specialist care must remain a national priority.”

articles.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
articles.summary: With fears of cyberattacks, conflict and major disruption to daily life grow in Europe, governments are urging citizens to prepare for emergencies. But in Britain, the culture of stockpiling supplies…

image.caption: A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting Intermarché and Cooperative U chains. Britain is among many European government introducing emergency preparedness campaigns. (Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The last time any British government launched a national public preparedness campaign was at the peak of the Cold War in 1980.

The “Protect and Survive” message was delivered in short, eerie-looking public information broadcasts and booklets, meant to advise people on how to prepare for a nuclear attack. The campaign — whose guidance included hiding under a heavy table or tips about how to store a dead body in the house for five days — backfired and was ridiculed. Brits realized little would protect them from a thermonuclear strike, leaving them feeling that preparation was pointless as survival would be futile.

Nearly 50 years on, the head of the British Army, Gen. Sir Roland Walker, addressed some 700 soldiers last month at Britain's biggest garrison in northern England. The "business of soldiering" had returned to the national psyche, he told members of the light, high-readiness global response force, adding that anyone following world affairs will realize there is “extreme jeopardy."

“The political leaders of this country,” he said, “will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country about just what is going on, and where the risk lies, and what the nation ... must need to be prepared to do.”

Exactly one week later, Britain’s “Be Ready” campaign was unveiled, a guide on preparing for 72 hours of self-sufficiency in the event of an emergency, be it a climate crisis, cyber disruptions or threats by hostile states.

“It’s something that emergency planners have been wanting for a very long time,” said Lucy Easthope, a global disaster recovery specialist. Easthope has advised in emergencies from the Novichok poisonings in Salisbury, England, to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and 9/11.
Easthope says what the public wants is reassurance — not negative and depressing messaging.
“Ancient DNA, by that I mean 30 years ago, is being reawoken,” she told CBC News. “This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable.
“I’m really pleased in the U.K. we haven’t resorted to fear messaging.”
Other European nations have also recently introduced or updated their emergency guidance, including France, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Germany and Poland.

Ottawa, too, has reiterated its longstanding advice. But unlike Canada with its emergency preparedness week — an annual event since 1996 — Britain faces a cultural hurdle, with the word "preparedness" not even being in most Brits' vocabulary. The U.K. has largely relied on community resilience to short-term disruptions, rather than self sufficiency. Now, it faces the challenge of convincing people that they must be prepared for the worst — without sending them into a panic.
Widespread warnings
In Hertfordshire, north of London, family physician Nyari Matebwe says her first reaction was to roll her eyes and ignore it.
“I feel like it’s scaremonger-y, or the skeptic in me thinks maybe they’re hiding something from us … another distraction from the real issues,” she said.

The recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers in multiple European countries and attempts to raise temperatures in French medical fridges containing critical blood donation stocks have made her question her own skepticism.
“After the recent airplane bomb hoaxes, I did start to think about it a bit more,” said Matebwe, whose teenage daughter is pushing her to take the prepping message seriously.
Sweden is advising seven days, Germany up to 10, but the U.K., like Canada, has settled on three days' survival off-grid.
Europe's wave of bomb threats spreads from airports to newsrooms
School parents’ WhatsApp groups are lighting up with conversations
“I want to stockpile but I’m in a state of inertia,” one parent wrote. “My husband is totally unbothered.”
Another asked, “How will we cook if there’s no gas or electricity?” while one raised concern about rising crime rates and the risk of keeping cash at home.
Warnings have been widespread recently.

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the government’s signals agency GCHQ and the Five Eyes intelligence sharing group that includes Canada, told CBC News: “This is a moment of urgency.”

items: Russia continues its attacks on power facilities in Kyiv as temperatures drop ahead of winter
The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?

blocks.text: The NCSC says AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the power stations, airports and hospitals in the U.K. within two years.
In Horne’s annual state of the cyber nation address, he said “military networks are subjected to sustained and persistent, widespread attempts to penetrate our systems."
That included Russian hybrid warfare campaigns, he said.
“All countries need to be taking this moment seriously," he told CBC News. “There are loads of vulnerabilities that do not need to be there,” which he said the country's adversaries are exploiting.
'Hard times have been forgotten'
Outside the need for companies to keep their technology safe, Horne said at home it is a case of keeping devices up to date and using passkeys.
“You do need to be thinking about, 'do I need to be having the levels of connectivity of devices across my house, apartment' … not unnecessarily introducing potential vulnerabilities.”
There are some who see the “Be Ready” messaging as another example of the "nanny state," or the government telling them how to live.
Others think cultural attitudes play a part.
Getting prepped to deal with emergencies
Luis Martinez Arnal, an IT professional from Spain now based in London, says his Mexican wife automatically prepares for emergencies, having grown up in a country prone to earthquakes.
“But in the U.K.,” Arnal said, “hard times have been forgotten.”
The accessibility of everything, he added, “psychologically is making us feel more comfortable.”

The recent cyberattacks have created a heightened sense of anxiety across Europe, and as people grow more reliant on the internet, questions are being asked how anyone can prepare to stay connected if it went down. Those haven't been easily answered — especially as Britain has long planned to switch all copper-wire landline phones to internet use-only from the end of January 2027.
“Call me crazy, but following the new guidelines, I do feel a bit nervous,” said one London mother, Amee Doshi, pointing to talk about the potential for a world war.

A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is seen stopped at a police roadblock on Sept. 27, in Fairford, U.K. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about 1.6 kilometres from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)
Others appear to be taking to it like true preppers.
“We bulk-buy,” said Preyal Shah, a working mother from Harrow in northwest London.
“I even now have 10 kilograms of rice, five kilograms of pasta … multiple cases of tinned food, each type being 12 tins.”
Preyal said she is also stockpiling newspapers to light a coal-burning stove: “Back to basics.”
Competing crises
In October, British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that the country needs to be “ready for war in 1,000 days," flagging the potential of Russian aggression.
“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” he said.
“We’ve just got so many competing crises at the moment … and war in Europe,” said Reena Patel, a lawyer from north London, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking war is coming but…” she said, listing off all she wants to buy, from a wind-up radio to water purification filters.
“The only thing I have in my control is to try to be a little bit prepared.”

articles.title: What needs to happen for Canada to join Europe's flagship student exchange program?
articles.summary: Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe. But how Canada would expand its participation…

image.caption: McGill University in Montreal is seen in 2023. Prime Minister Mark Carney said last month that once Canada becomes a partner country of Erasmus+, 'a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill.' (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe. But how Canada would expand its participation in Erasmus+ is complicated.
EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, but there are details Canada must iron out
Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe.

At last month's Canada-EU summit and in his 2026 budget, Prime Minister Mark Carney reaffirmed the government's interest in expanding Canada's participation in Erasmus+, Europe's internationally recognized student and skills exchange.
"Through this program, a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill," Carney said at the summit in Montreal.
An expert in European integration says the prospect is complex and likely to be expensive — but that it would come with major benefits for Canada's youth and deepening ties with the EU.

items: Carney wants Canada to join Europe's Erasmus+ program. What is it?

blocks.text: Through Erasmus+, students in the EU and select other countries have direct access to funding, institutions and grants that help cover travel and living costs when participating in exchange programs between institutions.
Students are also exempted from the fees for tuition, registration and exams that a Canadian exchange student might typically pay to study in Europe.

But Erasmus+ isn't just an opportunity for students. Its benefits extend to people starting their careers across a wide range of fields, including trainees, apprentices, youth workers and academic staff.
"An apprentice welder in Manitoba could bring or complete their placement with an employer in Italy, bringing new skills home," Carney said.
Many Canadian universities are already partnered with Erasmus+ through independent agreements, but they're limited mostly to exchange opportunities for master's students and faculty members.

Further participation in Erasmus+ could expand funding opportunities for undergraduates as well as youth, training and sport exchanges — all of which are available to EU members and the program's current six associate countries.
How would this work?
Oliver Schmidtke, a University of Victoria professor specializing in European integration, called Canada's proposed involvement in Erasmus+ "a lot of ambition."

"Education is largely a provincial thing in Canada, so how this would land and how the federal government would interact with provincial governments in trying to regulate this … that's a whole range of questions that are open," Schmidtke said.
What could EU associate membership look like for Canada?
And buying into an international exchange program isn't exactly cheap. The United Kingdom is rejoining in January and will pay over $1 billion for its first year.

Canadian universities would have to "pay substantial amounts to be eligible for the full array of services" and provide housing supports and staff to accommodate the Erasmus+ students coming to Canada, Schmidtke said.
The provinces and European Union would also have to iron out credit transfers for participating students — no simple feat.
All current Erasmus+ members and associated third countries follow the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS), simplifying the academic credit transfer process.
When the United Kingdom rejoins, it will be using its own system, but has set up a national framework for how credits will be transferred.
In Canada, even credit transfers between institutions within the same province aren't consistent.

items: Students across Ontario walk out to protest OSAP changes, tuition hike
Ontario estimated to lose more than a 3rd of its international students: StatsCan

blocks.text: This work would come at time of "a lot of financial stress at Canadian universities," Schmidtke said.
He said some of that comes from a reduced number of international students in Canada in recent years — who generally pay higher tuition rates directly to the institutions.

Carney has indicated that the expected costs of joining Erasmus+ won't stop Canada from pursuing that goal. Joining was one of the most concrete examples Carney gave when he announced in September that Canada was pursuing an "alliance for the future" with the EU.
"We don't view this as paying for something," Carney said in Montreal about the overall costs of closer EU integration. "We view this as coming together."

items: Why none of the EU's existing partnerships are the right fit for Canada

blocks.text: Despite these potential complications, Schmidtke believes integration with Erasmus+ will be an "invaluable opportunity" for Canadian students.

"Canada is a bit behind the curve when it comes to internationalizing student experiences, mobility and so forth," Schmidtke said. "So the Erasmus+ program could be a great incentive to expand the international experience of many Canadian students."
Some Canadian universities already involved

The University of Victoria, University of Waterloo, McMaster University, Simon Fraser University, University of Toronto, University of British Columbia and the University of Calgary told CBC News they would be open to exploring participation — or further participation, as some already partner with Erasmus+ — as more details become available.

Western University president Alan Shepard said international engagement is a key part of the student experience at Western, and the university was excited about the opportunities Erasmus+ could create.
"We encourage our students to see themselves as global citizens through opportunities to study, conduct research and gain hands-on experience around the world," Shepard said.
How Canadian students could benefit from EU 'associate member' status

In late October, Université Laval rector Sophie D'Amours and Sorbonne University president Nathalie Drach-Temam penned an open letter in La Presse encouraging the government to integrate Canadian universities into the program.

"The Sorbonne is the oldest French-language university in Europe. Université Laval is the oldest French-language university in the Americas. Our traditions are strong, as is our capacity to help address the challenges of tomorrow," the letter said.
By joining forces, we will be even better placed to promote the common good that universities represent for society."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sophia Laporte is an intern with CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa and a fourth-year journalism and humanities student at Carleton University.

articles.title: Injured Wainwright soldiers benefit from cutting-edge Canadian burn research
articles.summary: When news broke about the deadly training accident at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital with severe burns, Véronique Moulin knew she had to help. She is on the…

blocks.text: Canadian scientists grow skin substitute for CFB Wainwright fire survivors
When news broke about the deadly training exercise at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital with severe burns, Véronique Moulin knew she had to help.

Her research group is nearing the end of clinical trials on a ground-breaking process to reconstruct and manufacture a permanent, human-like skin substitute by taking a toonie-sized biopsy of the patient's healthy skin and extracting the cells.
"If everybody can survive and [I] can help to treat some, I will be happy," said Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre.
Unlike other lab-grown skin technologies, Moulin's method coaxes the patient's own cells to create a completely natural skin tissue containing both the dermis and epidermis layers.
Véronique Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre, is seen placing cells into liquid nitrogen for long-term preservation. (CBC)

While it's not completely identical to the patient's skin because it doesn't have pigment and sweat glands, Moulin said it's useful in cases where the burns cover too much of the body to harvest skin for grafts.

Clinical data on 50 Canadian burn patients treated since 2005 shows that, unlike grafts from cadavers, their body doesn't reject the skin substitutes. The tissue grows, fuses and stays flexible, which means less scarring and reduces the need for repetitive surgeries as the patient heals, she said.
Lab now growing skin from wounded soldiers

As of Nov. 4, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said 25 soldiers remain in hospital. Four have been moved to health-care facilities in British Columbia and Ontario to continue treatment closer to their home communities and families.
Skin biopsies from several of the hospitalized soldiers have been taken, and cells are now growing in Moulin's lab.
But it takes up to eight weeks to grow the first batch of skin substitute grafts from the initial biopsy — which is only enough to cover part of a torso — and her lab is already running at capacity.
"Usually we have three, sometimes four, but it's very rare that we have so many patients at the same time," Moulin said.
"But at least we can start, and after the first one, we can continue and send them every two weeks, we can send the same surface area."
Family of soldier severely burned at CFB Wainwright describes his ordeal
Burn research advancing across the country
Moulin is just one of the Canadians on the front lines of research meant to help burn patients heal faster, with less pain and fewer scars.

Halfway across the country, in a University of Manitoba lab, an interdisciplinary team of researchers is also developing skin substitutes that mimic the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors.

A close-up of the skin substitute that an interdisciplinary team of researchers is developing in a University of Manitoba lab. It mimics the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)

"Currently, we are working on one type of skin substitute that we are planning to test on animals. So that is the first step. You test on animals, then if it works, we will go to clinical trials," said Hamed Alizadeh Sardroud, a postdoctoral fellow and researcher in biomedical engineering and tissue engineering.

The lab is also exploring ways to engineer donor cells to be compatible with the recipient’s immune system and avoid rejection. They're using a 3D printer to create patches that would be used for burn wounds.
"Those cells are live and they can grow. And when you implant it, transplant [it] on the skin, they will just regenerate," Alizadeh Sardroud said.
3D printing skin substitutes for grafts
Just a few doors down, one of his colleagues is testing a biosensor that can detect bacteria causing infection in a wound.

items: Prolonged, fragile recovery ahead for soldiers severely burned at CFB Wainwright
‘Not an easy path’: Burn survivor reflects on long recovery facing soldiers injured in Wainwright fire

blocks.text: "You can see it's yellow and then as soon as it's in contact with bacteria and their enzymes, it becomes green," said Farinaz Jonidi Shariatzadeh, a post-doctoral researcher, as she did a demonstration.
"It's like an early warning system that shows you that the bacteria are present in the wound and … infection is going to start soon."
Infection detection and management

The postage stamp-sized nanofibre membrane can be placed in the top layer of a dressing so it doesn't have to be removed to keep an eye on the wound. A patient can monitor it at home, and contact their doctor when they see the colour change.
It has already been licensed by an American medical technology company that has begun clinical trials, Jonidi Shariatzadeh said.
"Compared to what's commercially available, it is groundbreaking because none of the available biosensors can actually show the colour change in real time that can be observed with the naked eye."

items: Family of injured Wainwright soldier holds bedside vigil in burn unit

blocks.text: The University of Manitoba team is also developing a smart dressing that will release an antibiotic as soon as an infection is detected, said Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre.
"The science fiction of yesterday is the treatment of today," he said.
"The goal is to decrease the pain and suffering and improve the quality of life and the quantity of life of individuals that have burns and also injuries of any kind."

Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre, leads a multi-disciplinary team of researchers that's become a hub for clinical innovation. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)
'The journey is a long and painful one'
It's welcome news for Tyler Pelke, who survived third-degree burns over 25 per cent of his body more than 35 years ago.

"The journey is a long and painful one," said Pelke, a former firefighter who is now a CAF reservist and head of Alberta's Emergency Health Services. He spoke as a burn survivor, not on behalf of those organizations.
"So yeah, some pretty amazing advancements, but it's a pretty impactful and horrific injury, especially when a large burn."
Pelke said he was lucky because doctors were able to take skin grafts from his own legs, but he dreaded the bandage removals and dressing changes.
Anything that can help ease the physical and mental suffering for burn patients is welcome, he said.

articles.title: Poilievre pans Liberal budget's $15M capital gains exemption, calls for 'simpler' plan
articles.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is criticizing a key feature of the Carney government's latest budget, arguing the proposed $15-million capital gains exemption on the sale of qualifying shares…

image.caption: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre rises after the tabling of the federal budget in the House of Commons, in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is criticizing a key feature of the Carney government's latest budget, arguing the proposed $15-million capital gains exemption on the sale of qualifying shares from a Canadian company applies too narrowly, excluding key businesses.
Conservative leader argues the range of qualifying businesses is too narrow
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 08, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 24 minutes ago

"Basically, I can't figure out who actually qualifies," Poilievre said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning. "I suspect no one does, and you have to be able to stand on one foot and count backwards from a thousand with your finger on your nose before you could qualify for that break."

In the 2026 federal budget, tabled on Thursday, the Canada Growth Incentive excludes businesses operating in the agricultural, fishing, forestry, financial, insurance, utilities, real estate, food and accommodation, arts, recreation and entertainment sectors.

Because of that, Poilievre said he views it as "insignificant and irrelevant and adds more complexity to the system." The budget states that the measure is expected to bring $715 million in tax relief over the next four years, beginning next fiscal year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal government is touting the incentive as a way to encourage Canadian founders to build a valuable company in Canada. Early-stage employees can receive more equity as part of their compensation, and investors get a better after-tax return for backing the business.
Budget 2026: Carney makes 'big bet' for investment, opposition blasts affordability moves
The budget calls the $15-million exemption "substantial" because founders would retain nearly 96 per cent of the company's value when they exit, compared with the current 71 per cent.

The move was met with praise by some business groups, including the Council of Canadian Innovators, which advocates on behalf of 175 high-growth companies in Canada. The group said the incentive would create the conditions companies need to attract talent and scale.
Poilievre did express support for Carney's productivity mega-deduction — expected to cost about $36 billion over five years — saying he believes anything that cuts taxes on investment is "positive."

items: Carney's 2nd budget earmarks billions for affordability and Canadian sovereignty

blocks.text: But Poilievre's approach would allow businesses and individuals that reinvest their capital gains back in Canada to fully defer the tax.

"And that would bring back the hundreds of billions of dollars of investment that companies and individuals have parked abroad.... I think that that would be economic rocket fuel. It would be a lot simpler than what Mr. Carney and the Liberals are proposing," the Opposition leader said.
Poilievre said he personally proposed the idea to Carney and encourages the prime minister to "steal my idea because we desperately need job-creating investment in Canada."
NDP criticizes affordability measures

The New Democrats have seized on the budget's tax cuts for new business investment, arguing that the affordability measures for Canadians pale in comparison. In a video statement posted on Thursday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis said, "If you're a billionaire, this budget is Christmas come early."

After the budget was read in the House of Commons by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, Lewis acknowledged it earmarks new funds to address homelessness but said it "doubles down on shovelling more money to the biggest CEOs and investors, with the promise that all of us will be better off for it. This has never worked."

Lewis also pointed out a chart in the budget that shows the spending composition of announced measures. In the chart, $98 billion is listed as "Growth and Investment," while $48 billion is listed as "People."
Champagne walked into the NDP leader's interview — and Lewis had questions

In an interview, Champagne said affordability is "top of mind" and that the budget boosts Canada's grocery benefit, extends the suspension of the federal excise tax on fuel and includes other measures on dental care and pharmacare.

"So we say two-thirds of the additional revenue we're getting, we're going to put that into growth and investments so that our economy will grow," the finance minister said. "But at the same time, we took one-third and we say, 'This is where we need to support people.'"
Poilievre criticized the government's borrowing, saying "government debt does not bring investment. It brings inflation, it brings stagnation and it brings failure."

items: From groceries to tax credits, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?
7 takeaways from the Carney government's 2nd budget

blocks.text: "We need to get the government out of the way and off the backs of Canadians so that we can have real free-enterprise growth that pays the bills and puts food on the table," the Conservative leader said.

Champagne told host Rosemary Barton that it will take time for the government's proposed tax cuts and productivity measures to translate into tangible benefits for everyday Canadians, but he was bullish on the impact the budget will have in due course.
"This is going to be making us stronger and more resilient," Champagne said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.

articles.title: How Trump's tariffs are threatening to spoil the success of Canadian cheese
articles.summary: In recent years, Canadian cheese has been having a bit of a moment south of the border, taking home some of the biggest awards in the Western hemisphere. But Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on certain…

image.caption: Grocery products line the shelves of a Vancouver supermarket in February 2025. U.S. tariffs on certain dairy products are hurting the success of Canadian cheese south of the border, industry stakeholders say. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

In recent years, Canadian cheese has been having a bit of a moment south of the border, taking home some of the biggest awards in the Western hemisphere. But Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on certain dairy products, including Canadian cheese, are threatening to spoil this success.
Heavy tariffs put the squeeze on award-winning products
In recent years, Canadian cheese has been having a bit of a moment south of the border, taking home some of the biggest awards in the Western hemisphere.

The turning point may have been in 2024, when Quebec's Fromagerie la Station won best in show at the American Cheese Society's annual competition out of hundreds of entries from both North and South America — and repeated the feat a year later.
Canadian cheeses were featured heavily among the winners at this year's awards as well.

"It just makes American consumers and people in the industry pay attention to something that they didn't realise was there before," said James Hanly, a sales director for Provisions International in Vermont, and one of the importers of Fromagerie la Station.
The string of awards got importers eager to bring in new, artisanal cheese from Canada that customers hadn't seen before, Hanly says.
"You know, people get excited about something new that is also shown to be high quality and delicious," he said in an interview with The Current.
But Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on certain dairy products, including Canadian cheese, are threatening to spoil this success.
LISTEN | Tariffs hurting Canadian cheese makers:
The Current21:27Trump’s 50% tariff is putting the squeeze on Canadian cheese
Since the tariffs went into effect this August, Hanly says demand for Canadian cheese has trailed off because of the increase in price.
"If the price becomes too expensive and customers stop buying it, and so the cheese shop or market stops bringing it in as well, you basically lose placement," he said.
Trump has repeatedly attacked Canada's dairy industry and its decades-old supply management system as being unfair to American dairy farmers, alleging Canada locks out U.S. dairy from its market.
But Hanly says the way Canada's dairy industry operates is part of what makes its cheese so great.
Canada operates on a dairy quota system, meaning producers will not be paid if they overproduce an abundance of milk.
Following their sweep of the midterm elections, Democrats say they'll work to revoke Trump's tariffs against Canada, which include a 50 per cent levy on certain dairy products. (Shane Hennessey/CBC)

"In the U.S, it's been a race to the bottom, trying to get the maximum amount of milk at the least amount of cost, which ends up producing lower quality milk that you can't use for cheese production," he said.

"Whereas in Canada with that closed circuit, you don't see that. You see, like, family farms thriving and succeeding and knowing what they're going to make. And so I think that stability and the quality of milk is what goes into that."
No other markets

The tariffs are weighing heavily on Mark Anderson, CEO of Mariposa Dairy in Lindsay, Ont., which has produced several cheeses that have earned top awards from the American Cheese Society in recent years.
With close to 80 per cent of their product exported to the U.S., the levies are posing a major threat to his business, and the 200 dairy goat farmers they purchase milk from.

"We haven't got the ability to turn that off. I mean those farmers count on us to take their milk, turn it into cheese, and get it to market. We don't really have any other markets that are like the U.S. that can take that kind of volume," Anderson told The Current.

items: Facing a potential $40M US tariff bill, this American importer is suing Trump to end some tariffs on Canada
Trump to swap some tariffs on Canadian goods amid midterm pressure

blocks.text: "So we're kind of forced to continue to keep our product on the shelf and find a way to work through these tariffs."
To avoid passing along additional costs to consumers, they've had to find a way to absorb them by working with their farmers, and distributor, the Gellert Global Group.
This U.S. company says it will fight Trump’s tariffs in court
"We're spreading it out so we could all take a little bit of the pain so we can last a little longer until this gets resolved," Anderson said.

Facing nearly $40 million in tariffs on the close to $80 million US worth of Canadian cheese it imports every year, the Gellar Global Group is currently suing the Trump administration to try to end some tariffs on Canadian products.
Anderson said the amount the tariffs could cost his business is "not too far off" that $40 million figure as well.
"It's phenomenal. It's not sustainable," he said.
However, with the Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in midterm elections earlier this week, both Hanly and Anderson say they're optimistic that the tide could be turning.
Senior Democrats have said the party will work to end Trump's tariffs on allies, including Canada, when the party takes control of Congress next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.
With files from The Current and Katie Simpson

articles.title: Freshwater species are at risk. A new global threat map could help save some from brink of extinction
articles.summary: A colourful new map that paints a not-so-rosy global picture of what's putting freshwater species at risk could help conservationists focus on threats and species most urgently in need of support.

image.caption: An Elisa skimmer dragonfly perches on a spiderweb-covered twig near a lake in northwestern Ontario in summer 2026. Dragonflies and damselflies represent one of five categories of freshwater wildlife around the world that researchers say is facing threats from a range of human activities. (Bryce Hoye

blocks.text: Science·New
A colourful new map that paints a not-so-rosy global picture of what's putting freshwater species at risk could help conservationists focus on threats and species most urgently in need of support.
Dams, farming, fishing, pollution, natural resource activity top Canada's threat list, McGill researcher says

There's no shortage of threats facing Canada's aquatic creatures — whether it's dam activity linked to endangered white sturgeon losses in B.C. rivers, toxic tailing pond water poisoning wood frogs in Alberta, or agricultural runoff and zebra mussels throwing Lake Winnipeg's ecosystem out of whack in Manitoba.
It's slipperier to determine which human activity is most responsible for putting freshwater biodiversity at risk more generally.

"We know that freshwater wildlife populations are declining faster than terrestrial or marine species, and we also know that wetlands are shrinking way faster than forests," said Christophe Brabant, a PhD candidate at McGill University.
"We generally know pretty well which threats are impacting freshwater species, we don't really know where those threats are happening across the world."

That's the piece of the puzzle Brabant and others set out to answer in new research published in the journal Science that maps out "the geography of threats" leading to freshwater biodiversity losses around the world.

They reviewed known threats to over 2,100 freshwater species on the "red list" created by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), which estimates a quarter of freshwater species are at risk of extinction. They then identified five groups of freshwater fauna facing risks — amphibians, reptiles, fish, mammals and odonates (dragonflies and damselfies).

Researchers created a global illustration of which threats appear to be the main drivers of declines. The result is a colour-coded map that shows threat intensity by region, and a companion index linking particular threats to declines in freshwater species.
"The map method … considers how different threats can affect different species rather than assuming that all species are affected equally," said Brabant.

The threat category with the highest impact in each subwatershed in the study shows a mosaic of differing threat intensities facing freshwater wildlife taxonomic groups across the world. (Submitted by Christophe Brabant et al.)

The activities topping Canada's threat list include: natural systems modification like dams and diversions, biological resource uses like hunting and fishing, agriculture, development, pollution, energy production and mining.
The leading threat identified globally was agriculture and aquaculture, particularly in the global south.
Pollution was the second most important threat category, especially in eastern China, India and across Europe.
Third was biological resource use, mostly in northern latitudes, including Canada and parts of sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia.
One of the main takeaways, Brabant says, is that there can't be "a one-size fits all solution" for conservation to be efficient.
Dr. Madison Earhart, left, steadies a white sturgeon in British Columbia in 2024 as part of ongoing research into threats facing Canada's largest freshwater fish. (submitted by Madison Earhart)
What also stood out is the "huge accumulation of threats" in northwestern Africa and Europe, the lower Himalayas and the Missouri River basin, says Brabant.
In places with relatively large proportions of species facing extinction, he says they also found that "most of our threats had a higher intensity."
Climate change
On the map, disease and invasive species are represented by a green band that extends across several provinces near the Canada-U.S. border. Both forces are exacerbated by global warming.
Climate change, which is listed as the main threat only in small pockets around the world, isn't the leading cause of declines in Canada, according to the research.
Researchers probe Manitoba wetlands for deadly frog, salamander disease
That could be more a reflection of limitations in the IUCN red list criteria to date than it is confirmation of climate change being a lesser threat, Brabant said.
"It's hard to know … that threat isn't recorded very well," he said.

One place it has been recorded well is at a network of kettle lakes in northwestern Ontario known as the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA), operated by the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD). There, scientists have been conducting experiments on real lakes since the 1960s to better understand how human activity impacts and threatens fresh water.

items: Manitoba fights U.S. project that could bring invasive species into Manitoba waters

blocks.text: The lakes are far from other confounding variables that make it harder to tease out whether climate change is a major driver of declines.
"We're only beginning to understand what climate change impacts are on various species in isolation," said Mike Rennie, a research fellow with the ELA.

Last year, Rennie and others published research based on decades of consistent data collection to monitor water quality and biodiversity of species in one of the "reference" lakes at the ELA that remained otherwise untouched.

A scientist draws a blood sample from a lake trout as part of a decades-long water quality and biodiversity monitoring program on one of 58 kettle lakes that make up the Experimental Lakes Area in northwestern Ontario. (Submitted by IISD Experimental Lakes Area)

Their work showed air temperatures in the area rose by about 2 C between 1986 and 2016, and the duration of ice coverage on the lake shrank by nearly three weeks. During the same period, Rennie says there was a "notable decline" in the size of adult lake trout.
These cold-water fish that rise from the depths to chow down on minnows when the shallows cool down in the winter now have less time and space to hunt near shore.

"Nothing else is going on except we're seeing these changes in things like ice cover," said Rennie, adding that such changes are "sort of our best indicator of how climate warming is impacting these small lakes and these cold water fish."
The Noah's Ark problem

Frederik Noack, the Canada Research Chair in environmental economics, acknowledges there are constraints, like budgets and other competing priorities, that complicate how information from the threat map is applied.
He says this often results in questions about what criteria should be used to target conservation efforts that would provide the biggest bang for the buck.

"Just knowing there's a high intensity of threats on endangered species doesn't necessarily make that the target of conservation funding," said Noack, who co-leads the Wildlife and Conservation Economics Laboratory at University of British Columbia.

A beaver trudges across snow and muck and into the Assiniboine River in Winnipeg as ice recedes this past spring. The mammal that was almost driven to extinction due to the fur trade is now considered stable in North America by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
He points to the Noah's Ark Problem, an economic model for biodiversity preservation from the late-1990s.

The analogy imagines how Noah, facing space constraints on the ark (think of this as the conservation budget), might choose which species survive and which are consigned to a watery grave, based on a desire to preserve as much overall biodiversity as possible while also factoring in the utility of each species to humanity and how likely they are to be rescued.
Noack notes the approach is very simplified, "but I think at least it gets the components right."

items: Toxic algae research goes viral on Lake Winnipeg

blocks.text: Critics of the model point to how it imagines species in isolation rather than sufficiently prioritizing the ecological role a given species plays that broadly benefits others.
The long-term survival of northern leopard frogs or Pacific salmon might depend on having a couple beavers aboard the arc to create wetland habitats other animals need to survive.

A frog lurks along the edges of a lake near the border of Manitoba and Ontario in September 2026. The IUCN red list estimates 25 per cent of global freshwater species are at risk of extinction. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
As the story goes, Noah was instructed to only reserve space for land-dwelling creatures and birds.
Brabant says biodiversity conservation frameworks also overlook freshwater species.
He hopes the maps raise the profile of freshwater creatures and help decision-makers focus in on areas that most urgently need support.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.
