blocks.text: DETAINED. Paraguay's former president Santiago Pena and his lawyer Ricardo Preda sit with judge Humberto Otazu, a day after Pena was impeached and placed under house arrest amid a political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of digital lender Ueno, in Asuncion, Paraguay, November 7, 2026.
Palacio de Justicia Paraguay/Handout v

Prosecutors allege that Santiago Peña used his position as president to influence decisions by government agencies and state-owned entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited with a digital lender he has ties to

items: Former Paraguayan president Santiago Peña has been ordered into pretrial detention while prosecutors investigate his connections to the collapsed digital lender ueno, which has affected millions of customers.
Peña faces charges of breach of trust and administration for personal gain, with allegations that he influenced government decisions to benefit ueno despite having financial ties to the lender.

The political and financial crisis following Peña's removal from office has led to protests and the detention of other officials, including former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, amid ongoing investigations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

A Paraguayan judge on Saturday, November 7, ordered former president Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility while prosecutors investigate his ties to digital lender ueno, whose collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts.

Judge Humberto Otazú ordered Peña, who has been charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, held at the facility, saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country while the case proceeded.

The detention, a day after Peña’s removal from office, deepens a political and financial crisis that has prompted protests in Asuncion, swept up senior officials and led regulators to try to contain risks to the wider financial system.
Peña’s attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that Peña was pleading not guilty to the charges.
“We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal,” Preda said.

Otazú also ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to pretrial detention in a holding center after prosecutors charged him with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment.

Prosecutors allege that Peña used his position as president to influence decisions by government agencies and state-owned entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at ueno, despite maintaining financial ties to the lender. They say that relationship created a conflict of interest as Peña encouraged, facilitated or influenced decisions benefiting the bank.
Peña, who was a shareholder in ueno’s holding company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter.

Peña had arrived at the Attorney General’s Office earlier on Saturday to appear before prosecutors following his dramatic removal from power on Friday. His ouster brought Vice President Pedro Alliana to power, with the longtime ruling Colorado Party politician sworn in on Friday to complete Peña’s term through August 2028.
The two charges against Peña could carry a sentence of up to 10 years in prison each, said prosecutor Nancy Salomón.
Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier this week as the crisis surrounding ueno escalated. He had previously headed the digital lender until 2023.
The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers, under the state deposit guarantee scheme. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints
articles.summary:
MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to

“It started as a trickle in 2024 and…

blocks.text: “It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.”

At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required.

That was until the rapid growth of ChatGPT – which turns four later this month – Claude, Copilot, Gemini and other generative AI tools over the past couple of years. These chatbots are helping turn laypeople into experts by giving access to a free – albeit sometimes unreliable – legal adviser, administrator or personal assistant.

The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth.

blocks.caption: ‘Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,’ says Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in an MP’s office. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload, at a time of already stretched resources.
This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters.
‘Everyone’s got a free lawyer’
With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence.

These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI.

“Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.”

Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says.

blocks.caption: Before AI, objecting to a local planning application would have taken some time and effort.  Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points.

“It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.”

The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested.

Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says.
Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans.

AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.”

blocks.caption: Complaints to local authorities are surging, including over issues such as planning applications, parking tickets and bin collections.  Photograph: Fotomaton/Alamy

blocks.text: Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case.

“Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.”
Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard.

The number of employment tribunal claims opened between April and June soared by 28% compared with a year earlier, representing 14,000 cases from single claimants, according to the most recent government figures. The number of concluded cases also fell during the quarter, resulting in 70,000 open single claims at the end of June.

The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools.
after newsletter promotion
The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”.

Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.”

blocks.caption: Transport for London (TfL) received a record 4,769 freedom of information requests in 2025-26, with a ‘noted increase’ in appeals believed to be AI-generated.   Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence.

Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24.

The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”.
Westminster inundated
The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope.

Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says.

She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests.

The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.”

blocks.caption: ‘AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,’ says Lisa Gillmore of the GMB union. ‘Casework has doubled or more.’ Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached.

Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it.

Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information.

Researchers have also suggested authorities could attempt to stem the AI flood by making it harder for people to complete applications, by charging fees for submitting requests or blocking bots from government websites.

The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions.

The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

articles.title: From the overblown to the ordinary? Met Gala 2027 to celebrate ‘poetics of everyday’
articles.summary:
Event regarded as Oscars of fashion industry replaces John Galliano retrospective with homage to the ‘extra ordinary’

A few months after the planned John Galliano Met Gala retrospective was…

blocks.text: A few months after the planned John Galliano Met Gala retrospective was cancelled amid a backlash focused on the designer’s past, a more commonplace theme has been announced: “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday.” It has left some commentators speculating that celebrities might replace the couture “omelette dresses” and four-part red-carpet performances with jeans and a nice top.
While the dress code for the next Met Gala, which will be held on 3 May 2027, is yet to be announced, it traditionally derives from the exhibition theme.

blocks.caption: A Dior haute couture gown designed by John Galliano displayed at the Louvre in Paris. Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/Reuters

blocks.text: According to a press release, extraORDINARY will “explore how designers rework familiar garments, everyday objects, and commonplace materials”. Taking wardrobe staples and everyday materials – “from jeans, T-shirts and puffer coats to paper, plastic and metal” – it will “examine how design reveals unexpected possibilities within everyday things”.

Reactions have been mixed. For Dana Thomas, the author of Gods and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano, it “reinforces the message that was very, very clear with the Galliano announcement that the costume institute’s team is highly out of touch”. She characterises the decision to “take such ordinary garments and then show how fashion has co-opted them and added zeros to the price tag” as tone deaf.

blocks.caption: Cher, with the fashion designer Bob Mackie wearing his ‘naked’ dress, attends the Met Gala in 1974. Photograph: Ron Galella Collection/Getty

blocks.text: It is also, she says, a “missed opportunity”. Thomas is among those who think the theme would have been better off honouring some of the biggest names from the worlds of fashion and popular culture who have died this year, including Dolly Parton and Bob Mackie, the designer responsible for the “naked” dress worn by Cher to the Met Gala in 1974 and many of Parton’s costumes over the years. “There could have been a Bob Mackie room in the Dolly Parton show.” It would, she says, “have been easy and it would have been a beautiful homage to a woman who was a style icon and a humanitarian”.

Thomas also thinks it would have “been enormous – it would have made the museum a ton of money, it would have gotten a lot of goodwill from the press. It would have been loved by Americans and tourists in New York alike.” Instead, she says, “fun is missing from the equation”.

According to 1Granary, a platform known for holding the industry to account: “The new Met Gala theme proves that sometimes fashion is either too controversial to exist or too boring to care about.” For Malique Morris, a correspondent at Line Sheet, an industry newsletter, his underwhelm stems from the fact it came “in the wake of a Galliano exhibit”. “Because we’re not getting that, we’re going to feel robbed,” he says.

Others online point out that this new theme feels about as far from the fantastical work of the famed couturier Galliano, who was found guilty of a hate crime in 2011 after a series of racist and antisemitic rants, as it’s possible to get.

blocks.caption: Da’Vine Joy Randolph attends the 2024 Met Gala in an all-denim creation designed by Zac Posen. Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty

blocks.text: But for some commentators, extraORDINARY is cause for celebration and intrigue. According to the celebrity stylist and Vogue contributor Marian Kwei, the theme is “very clever”. It seems, she says, “very simple, but it’s far from it. It’s actually a very interesting thing, which I think is an incredible celebration of fashion, the concept of fashion design and what designers try to do with design itself.”

As for how the theme could translate on to the red carpet: “it could be a palette cleanser,” says Morris, “maybe a bit of a refresh. Instead of the constant peacocking, trying to have a viral moment … there could be a sense of just look good, make sure the clothes fit you well, tell a story and that story doesn’t have to be incredibly high glam.”

There is a red carpet precedent for staples like denim. The American designer Zac Posen, in his capacity as creative director of Gap, has been responsible for lots of these trends, including at the Met. In 2024 Da’vine Joy Randolph wore an all-denim creation by Posen to the gala. At last year’s event, the Australian pop star Troye Sivan wore devoré-effect jeans by Prada and the model Bhavitha Mandava wore muslin-printed trousers made to look like blue jeans by Matthieu Blazy at Chanel.

blocks.caption: The Australian singer Troye Sivan wears Prada jeans at the 2026 Met Gala. Photograph: Daniel Cole/Reuters

blocks.text: Perhaps the exhibition’s focus on “recycling, upcycling and reuse” will see the work of designers such as the Swedish designer Ellen Hodakova Larsson, who creates couture gowns out of belt buckles and old spoons, worn to the event. Kwei speculates that the work of the Dutch designer Duran Lantink, who does “incredible things with everyday materials”, may be a good fit.

With individual tickets last year going for about $100,000, there is nothing everyday about the guest list, which is personally overseen by Anna Wintour. There are, says Kwei, opportunities for missteps “when it is attended by people who are not really in touch with the context of the times”. It is, she says, “going to be very interesting for the red carpet”.

articles.title: Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts
articles.summary:
Naturalists divided over potential impact of proposals to increase number of wild raptors in England and Wales

White-tailed eagles reintroduced into England and Wales imperil…

blocks.text: White-tailed eagles reintroduced into England and Wales imperil endangered seabird populations and risk wiping out some colonies, ecologists and conservationists are warning.

Puffins, guillemots, razorbills, fulmars and kittiwakes are among the birds for which breeding populations could collapse if large numbers of white-tailed eagles are released, according to some academics and conservationists.

“Amidst all the excitement and enthusiasm for reintroducing white-tailed eagles, the fact that these birds will probably destroy our seabird colonies seems to have been completely overlooked,” said Tim Birkhead, an emeritus professor of ecology and evolution at the University of Sheffield.

The return of white-tailed eagles to Britain after they were driven to extinction in 1918 has been a great conservation success story in recent decades. But proposals to release up to 60 eagles in Gwent, south Wales, on top of 20 young birds already being released over the next three years on Exmoor, is dividing nature lovers.
The Gwent Wildlife Trust is supporting the proposed Gwent reintroduction while the Wildlife Trust of South & West Wales (WTSWW) is opposed.

Last month an eagle from the Exmoor release was sighted over the south Wales island of Skomer, a renowned seabird sanctuary where David Attenborough was filmed encountering puffins and shearwaters for his Wild Isles series. British seabirds have suffered the worst declines of any group of birds over the last five years, with populations falling by a fifth, but the seabird populations in south Wales are relatively healthy.

blocks.caption: White-tailed eagles can pose a risk to seabirds but some conservationists argue a balance needs to found with other potential opportunities. Photograph: Risto Juvaste/BirdLife Finland

blocks.text: Sarah Kessell, the chief executive of WTSWW, said: “We’re increasingly alarmed about the reintroduction of white-tailed eagles across the UK as more evidence comes to light of their impact on cliff-nesting seabirds.

“The islands of Skomer and Skokholm are a sanctuary for globally important seabird populations, which are already under threat. The extra pressure of disturbance and displacement from white-tailed eagles could have a significant impact on breeding seabirds. We have an overwhelming obligation to protect the seabirds on the islands that we manage.”

White-tailed eagle chicks brought over from Norway to reintroduce them into Scotland in 1975 has led to a wild population now of 200 breeding pairs, with 45 birds successfully reintroduced to the Isle of Wight since 2019. Although there has been repeated illegal killing of the huge avian predator, the first English-born wild bird fledged from a nest in East Sussex in 2023. Wales has not yet restored the species to its skies.

Prof Geoff Hilton, the head of wetland evidence at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT), which is leading the Gwent reintroduction, said: “Conservation action has and always will carry an element of risk. But what’s essential is that we carefully evaluate those risks early, use robust evidence to investigate the scale of those risks, and balance them against potential opportunities.”

Hilton emphasised that white-tailed eagles were generalist feeders with a varied diet including carrion, fish and small mammals. Research published in 2020 of eagles east of the Baltic Sea found that birds of particular conservation concern in the EU accounted for approximately 1% of identified prey in a long-term study of eagle diets.

He said: “With careful phasing, we aim to establish seven to nine breeding pairs of white-tailed eagles over the next 10 years. Therefore, we don’t expect this reintroduction to significantly reduce or impact any single species population. We do, however, expect to see healthier, more balanced ecosystems and landscapes, as apex predators like these eagles start to thrive once again.”

blocks.caption: Guillemots on Skomer Island off the coast of Pembrokeshire in Wales. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/D Legakis Photography/Athena

blocks.text: In evidence submitted by WTSWW against the Gwent proposals, Stephen Votier, a professor of seabird conservation and ecology at Heriot-Watt University, said: “It is clear that white-tailed eagles can have severe impacts on seabird populations – they seem especially vulnerable because the eagle can indirectly affect social aspects of breeding.”

As well as directly predating seabirds and their young, indirect effects are likely to be much greater, say some researchers, because the fear induced by white-tailed eagles causes adult seabirds to temporarily desert their breeding sites, exposing chicks to predation by other birds including gulls and corvids.

Birkhead, who has studied the guillemot population on Skomer since 1972, said he would “love to see white-tailed eagles” but said scientific evidence of the predators hastening the extinction of seabird colonies in Scandinavia must be properly considered.

In 2023, a scientific paper found that in northern Norway an increasing abundance of white-tailed eagles accelerated the loss of a kittiwake colony in Røst in 2020 by “many years”. The colony was already in decline but the eagles’ impacts were greater because fewer fish for the kittiwakes compelled the birds to spend more time foraging and less time defending their young from predators.

Annette Fayet and Tycho Anker-Nilssen, co-authors of the study, said that although Røst only had two to three breeding pairs of eagles, large numbers of immature eagles gathered there and disturbed the nesting seabirds.

Asked about the applicability of their findings to Wales, they said: “We cannot assume that the situation in Norway will be reproduced in south Wales but find it impossible to rule out that something similar could happen there too, in time.”

Roger Morgan-Grenville, the author of a book about white-tailed eagles that will be published next spring, said there was a consistent association between the rising number of white-tailed eagles on the Baltic coast and the reduced breeding success of the cormorant, and similar negative impacts on northern gannets and kittiwakes in western Norway. He said: “I’m absolutely in favour of these magnificent birds covering our skies again but we need to listen to all voices, and not just the loud ones, and we need to accept that the landscape that the white-tailed has come back into is a far more depleted one than it left in 1918.”

Natural Resources Wales is assessing the application for the release of white-tailed eagles in Gwent, with a verdict expected by the end of this year. A spokesperson said: “If we are minded to grant a licence, there will be a public consultation process from late 2026 into early 2027 before any final decision is made.”

articles.title: Pedro Taduran retains world crown by clear unanimous decision
articles.summary: Pedro Taduran, the pride of Libon, Albay, still stands as the Philippines' sole world boxing champion after a decisive win over Brandon Moreno of Spain

blocks.text: STILL THE CHAMP. Filipino boxing champion Pedro Taduran celebrates his successful title defense against Brandon Moreno of Spain.
Jhay Otamias
Pedro Taduran, the pride of Libon, Albay, still stands as the Philippines' sole world boxing champion after a decisive win over Brandon Moreno of Spain

items: Pedo Taduran won a unanimous decision against Brandon Moreno, retaining his IBF minimum weight title.
Taduran applied relentless pressure throughout the fight, ultimately outworking Moreno, who suffered his first career loss.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – There was no knockdown, only a convincing unanimous decision for Pedro Taduran.

Applying relentless pressure, Taduran trounced Brandon Moreno of Spain by scores of 120-108, 115-113, and 115-113 to retain the IBF (International Boxing Federation) minimumweight crown and remain the lone Filipino world champion on Saturday, November 7 (Sunday, November 8, Philippine time) at the Kiva Auditorium in Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA.
The heavy-hitting Taduran said he didn’t find the opening to put Moreno down and settled for outworking and wearing down the erstwhile unbeaten challenger.
“It was a bit hard (to knock him down) as he throws punches before I could come in. I made my move when I felt that he was losing steam,” Taduran told Rappler in Filipino.
Living up to his favorite tag, Taduran improved to a 21-win, with 14 knockouts, 4-loss, 1-draw record, while handing the Spaniard his first loss after 16 wins with 5 knockouts.
Although two inches shorter at 5-foot-3, Taduran was the aggressor from the start, with Moreno keeping him at bay with jabs.
Once Taduran found his rhythm and unloaded punches in bunches, however, Moreno began to open up and get hit.
Joven Jimenez manned Taduran’s corner with his ward, former IBF junior bantamweight king Jerwin Ancajas.

According to Jimenez, they had to compress everything in two weeks as Taduran was overweight (126 pounds) and undertrained when he started working out at the Knuckleheads Boxing Gym in Las Vegas, Nevada.

Taduran, the pride of Libon, Albay, said he will head to Las Vegas on Sunday and will return to the Philippines by Tuesday, adding that MP Promotions president and matchmaker Sean Gibbons will work out his next fight.

image.caption: Delhi residents woke up Sunday to 'very unhealthy' levels of air pollutionImage: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

blocks.text: November 8, 2026
Delhi most polluted city in world on Diwali eve

blocks.caption: People in the capital woke up to a thick smog as pollution worsened in DelhiImage: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

blocks.text: Delhi awoke Sunday morning enveloped in smog with poor visibility after the previous night saw the worst air quality for Diwali eve in 10 years.
The worst polluted pre-Diwali day was in 2016 when on October 29 the air quality index hit 404 on India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
On Saturday, the day before Diwali, Swiss ​group IQAir had ranked Delhi as the world's most polluted major city.
IQAir said Delhi had a "very unhealthy" air quality index (AQI) of 201 on Sunday.
The air quality is forecast to turn "severe" on Sunday, with Diwali celebrations adding to the pollution.

While vehicular emissions and stubble burning in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana are major contributors to air pollution, Diwali celebrations, which involve large-scale burning of firecrackers, add to the pollution in the city.
The government had already ordered schools in and ​around Delhi to offer online classes, and ​encouraged people to work from home ahead of ⁠the Hindu festival of light.

articles.title: Strawberry cansi? Art meets food at Mt. Camisong for Ibagiw 2026
articles.summary: For Ibagiw 2026, chef Stanley Suva and artist Amparo Moldero-Magallanes bring together food, memory, and Cordillera creativity in a collaboration that gives familiar ingredients and old materials new…

blocks.text: BENGUET, Philippines — It began with a painting of a paper boat caught in a fishing net, surrounded by fish and swirling waves. Chef Stanley “Stan” Suva saw it and he immediately remembered a kilawin dish he had created years earlier.
Artist Amparo Moldero-Magallanes had not painted Of Dreams Cast at Sea with Suva’s dish in mind. But the resemblance was striking enough that he pulled out his phone to show her.
It was one of the happy coincidences that made their collaboration for the ninth Ibagiw Creative Festival feel special.

At Alapaap Dining in Mt. Camisong Forest Park, art has returned to the dinner table for another year of Gastro X Art, pairing chefs and visual artists to explore the relationship between food and creative expression.
This year, Suva, Mt. Camisong’s vice president for food and beverage, is paired with Moldero-Magallanes, a Baguio artist and apothecary whose paintings are playful and personal.
Their project, Roots in Transformation, is part of Ibagiw 2026’s theme, RIKUS: A Creative Circular Baguio, which explores sustainability, renewal, and the creative reuse of materials.
But this collaboration goes beyond matching paintings with beautifully plated food.

blocks.caption: MATCH. Chef Stanley Suva and artist Amparo Moldero-Magallanes present their kilawin alongside Of Dreams Cast at Sea. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: The first surprise came with the kilawin.
The familiar Filipino dish had a welcome addition: camote. Its sweetness and texture worked remarkably well with the acidity of the kilawin, making an already enjoyable dish more interesting.
The kilawin was paired with Moldero-Magallanes’ Of Dreams Cast at Sea, a watercolor-and-ink illustration of fish, waves, and a fishing net carrying a paper boat.
The pairing was meaningful because neither artist nor chef had created their work for the other.
Another dish, Pinoy Chicken BBQ with Smoked Pineapple Salsa, came with a clever take on rice.

The familiar tutong, the browned rice that forms at the bottom of a cooking pot, was reimagined as Pinoy ampaw, a crispy rice cake made with Unoy heirloom rice from Pasil, Kalinga. Its crunch complemented the chicken barbecue and smoked pineapple salsa.
The dish was inspired by Moldero-Magallanes’ Of Crispy Steps and Borrowed Flight, a playful illustration of children, a paper boat, and a chicken against swirling colors and mountain forms.
Then came the strawberry cansi.
Cansi, a beef soup traditionally associated with Western Visayas, gets its sourness from batwan. Suva’s version introduces Benguet strawberries, bringing a distinctly local ingredient into the broth.
The result was addictive: the soup’s tang and the strawberries’ sweetness made for an unusual combination that worked.
Suva has explained that the restaurant uses underripe strawberries, less suited for desserts, in its cansi. It is one way the kitchen makes use of ingredients that might otherwise go to waste.
The accompanying artwork, Of a Strawberry and a Floating Cow, features a strawberry hanging beneath a fanciful scene of clouds, mountains, and a floating cow.
Dessert brought another surprise.

The chocolate mousse came with a rose element that added freshness to the rich chocolate. Inspired by Of Leather Towers and Sweet Rivers, the dish played with layered textures, with the fruit leather and mousse echoing the painting’s towers and flowing forms.
It was a lovely end to a meal that kept us curious about what would arrive next.

blocks.caption: ART. Moldero-Magallanes’ paintings adorn the walls of Alapaap Dining at Mt. Camisong, bringing her imaginative landscapes, colors, and storytelling into the restaurant. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: There is a personal story behind the paintings.
Moldero-Magallanes grew up with artist parents and began painting as a child. As life and work took over, however, her creative pursuits gradually moved into the background.
For years, her artwork appeared on the packaging of products from her small business. Upon reaching her golden years, she decided it was time to return to painting and share her work more widely.
She describes her style as whimsical and dreamlike, shaped by her parents’ influence and her desire to bring viewers back to simpler, happier memories.
For this year’s collaboration, she also experimented with materials that might otherwise have been discarded.

Expired Abra dyes became watercolor palettes, while rejected materials from soap production were turned into paint. Old glitter dyes were incorporated into acrylics, and existing canvases were given new life.
Her background in medical technology, she explained, helped shape her resourcefulness and willingness to experiment.
Moldero-Magallanes also spoke warmly about the chefs she and her husband have befriended over the years.
She has long believed that chefs are artists in their own right, not only because of how food looks, but also because they create experiences through taste, texture, and memory.
A dish, she observed, can remind someone of a mother’s cooking or a particular moment in life.
Watching Suva connect his earlier kilawin with her painting gave that belief a personal meaning.

blocks.caption: FUSION. Pinoy Chicken BBQ with Smoked Pineapple Salsa is served with ampaw, made from Unoy heirloom rice from Pasil, Kalinga, and inspired by the familiar tutong. The dish is paired with Moldero-Magallanes’ Of Crispy Steps and Borrowed Flight, an illustration featuring children, a chicken, and a…

blocks.text: Suva shares her view of cooking. As a chef, he sees food as a form of artistic expression, with ingredients and cooking techniques serving much the same purpose as an artist’s materials and tools.
His interest in Moldero-Magallanes’ work deepened when he learned how she incorporated recycled materials into her paintings.
At Alapaap, his kitchen has been working to reduce food waste and find more uses for available ingredients.
Their collaboration offered a chance to bring these approaches together.
Mt. Camisong board chairperson Ludette Querubin acknowledged that sustainability remains a work in progress.
The organization, she said, continues to learn and improve its practices through partnerships with artists, chefs, and the surrounding community.
For Querubin, sustainability extends beyond environmental concerns to food, culture, livelihoods, and the people who make these initiatives possible.
That broader perspective is relevant in the Cordillera, where resourcefulness and making use of available materials have long been part of everyday life.

The collaboration also points to a possible direction for Baguio’s creative economy. Artists can reach new audiences through dining, while chefs introduce guests to local ingredients, cultural stories, and the work of other creatives.
Such collaborations could benefit both, provided they give participating artists meaningful recognition and support.

blocks.caption: SWEET. A rose adds an unexpected floral touch to Chef Suva’s chocolate mousse, paired with Moldero-Magallanes’ Of Leather Towers and Sweet Rivers. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Gastro X Art has returned to Ibagiw, and this year’s pairing at Mt. Camisong shows why the collaboration deserves to continue.
The dishes were enjoyable on their own. What made the meal memorable was discovering the stories behind them, then looking at the paintings again and noticing details we had missed earlier.
The art did not feel like decoration added to a restaurant. Nor did the food seem like an afterthought to an exhibition.
Suva and Moldero-Magallanes found a way to let their individual works speak to each other, sometimes by design and, as with the kilawin, through coincidence.

Roots in Transformation runs from November 8 to 30, 2026, at Alapaap Dining in Mt. Camisong Forest Park, Sitio Peday, Barangay Loacan, Itogon, Benguet, as part of the Ibagiw Gastro X Art + Live Music Creative Crawl.
If you happen to visit, don’t rush through the meal. Look at the paintings, listen to the stories, and give the food your full attention.
Especially the strawberry cansi. I’d happily have another bowl. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Cempaka' expected to intensify into typhoon before entering PAR
articles.summary: As of 10 a.m. on Sunday, November 8, the center of Cempaka was located 1,720 kilometers east of Extreme Northern Luzon, remaining outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 3:45pm
Satellite photo of severe tropical storm “Cempaka” as of 10:40 a.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.
PAGASA / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Severe Tropical Storm “Cempaka” maintained its strength while moving westward over the Philippine Sea east of Extreme Northern Luzon on Sunday, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.
As of 10 a.m. on Sunday, November 8, the center of Cempaka was located 1,720 kilometers east of Extreme Northern Luzon, remaining outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).
The cyclone carries maximum sustained winds of 110 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center, with gusts reaching up to 135 kph and a central pressure of 990 hPa.
It is currently moving westward at a speed of 25 kph, with strong to storm-force winds extending outward up to 380 kilometers from its center.
PAGASA expects Cempaka to continue moving west-northwestward and enter the PAR between Sunday evening and early Monday morning, November 9.
Upon entry, the tropical cyclone will be given the local name "Samuel".

However, the storm is expected to have a brief stay within the region. It is projected to veer north-northeastward by Monday afternoon or evening before exiting through the northeastern boundary of the PAR.
The state weather bureau expects Cempaka to intensify into a typhoon on Sunday and continue strengthening toward its peak intensity before gradually weakening starting Tuesday, November 10.
Because the tropical cyclone will remain over the Philippine Sea, far from land, PAGASA stated that it is not expected to directly affect weather or sea conditions across the country.
Nevertheless, the Northeast Monsoon, locally known as “amihan,” will bring moderate to rough seas over the seaboards of Northern and Central Luzon over the next 24 hours.
Very rough seas are anticipated along Northern Luzon's seaboards starting Tuesday, with a Gale Warning likely to be issued on Monday.

articles.title: Erwin Tulfo files bill seeking worker protection vs. layoffs due to AI
articles.summary: Senator Erwin Tulfo filed a bill seeking to protect workers from artificial intelligence-driven layoffs by amending the Labor Code to establish clear conditions for terminations and guarantee fair…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 3:01pm

Senator Erwin Tulfo filed a bill seeking to protect workers from artificial intelligence-driven layoffs by amending the Labor Code to establish clear conditions for terminations and guarantee fair compensation.

Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Social Justice, Welfare, and Development, introduced Senate Bill (SB) No. 2563, which proposes key amendments to Article 298 of the Labor Code of the Philippines.

“As companies adopt AI, employees whose jobs become redundant risk losing not only their employment but also their means of supporting their families. Technological progress is inevitable, but Filipino workers should not be left behind or made it bear its costs alone,” Tulfo wrote in his explanatory note.

In a statement on Sunday, the senator said SB No. 2563 requires employers to provide fair separation pay, opportunities for reskilling and redeployment, and advance notice with mandatory consultations for affected workers.
Under the bill, employers can only terminate workers due to AI automation if the following conditions are met:

items: There must be a bona fide introduction of implementation of AI technologies or systems;
AI implementations must be undertaken in good faith;
The purpose for AI introduction or implementation is valid to save cost, enhance efficiency and other justifiable economic reasons;
No other option available for the employer other than to introduce or implement AI technologies and the consequent termination of employee; and
There must be fair and reasonable criteria in selecting employees to be terminated.

blocks.text: Should terminations occur, the bill requires employers to notify the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) at least six months in advance.

It also stipulates that employees terminated under these conditions are entitled to separation pay equal to at least two months pay or to at least two months pay for every year of service, whichever is higher.
Tulfo stressed that before turning to AI automation, employers must first exhaust all efforts to reskill their existing workforce before resorting to layoffs.

“There must be a proactive effort to keep workers away from termination just because AI comes in. We are not only talking about careers here, we are concerned with livelihood and lives of the employees’ families,” the senator said.
Malacañang meanwhile on Friday admitted that AI may displace workers. However, the technology could also bring new opportunities for Filipinos. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Banana producers in Latin America want better pay to cope with effects of climate crisis
articles.summary:
Farmers face big drop in production from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event

Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of…

blocks.text: Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.

High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.

Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.

Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.

Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.

“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.

Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”

Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.
While some businesses, including Sainsbury’s, the Co-op and Waitrose, have taken voluntary steps by sourcing only Faitrade bananas, which guarantee a minimum price, it says there is more work to do.

Eleanor Harrison, the chief executive of Fairtade, said: “The UK’s banana supply depends on the people growing our bananas having the resources they need to adapt to climate change, and to invest in their future. Fair prices, climate resilience and decent work go hand in hand.”
after newsletter promotion
While bananas are becoming harder and more expensive to produce, supermarket prices have remained unchanged for almost 40 years despite rising costs for fertiliser, fuel and labour.

Caoimhe Buckley, the chief corporate affairs officer at the large supplier Fyffes, said: “The long-term sustainability of the banana sector … cannot be separated from purchasing practices. The price of bananas in the supermarket needs to recognise the real and sustainable cost of production, including labour and decent wages, environmental management, human-rights due diligence and the investment necessary to adapt to climate change.”
Research by the Ethical Trading Initiative found that prices paid to suppliers in 2026 did not even cover basic production costs for 66.7% of them.

It said producers need more help to adapt or mitigate climatic changes, which could mean suitable land for banana cultivation could shrink by an average of 61% across Latin America and the Caribbean by 2050, according to research for the Inter-American Development Bank published in 2020.

articles.title: 2027 budget bicam proceedings transcripts to be released, will help track realignments - Lacson
articles.summary: The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027, Senator Panfilo Lacson said…

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:55pm

The Senate will release transcripts of the discussions during the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 202, Senator Panfilo Lacson said Sunday.
In a statement, Lacson said the transcript would help lawmakers and the public track who pushed for realignment of specific items in the budget.
“Kailangan may minutes ‘yan para maliwanag sino nag-initiate ng amendment at sino nagtulak ng realignment,” Lacson said.
(There should be a transcript containing the minutes so it will be clear who initiated amendments and who pushed for realignments.)
He added that the Senate is also pushing for continued livestreaming of the bicam conference committee discussions.

Aside from continuing transparency measures from the 2026 budget, Lacson said the Senate also plans to identify senators who proposed amendments to the budget bill and posting the proceedings on the Senate’s website.
For the 2027 budget, Lacson said the Senate plans to invite budget advocacy groups like the People’s Budget Coalition to the bicameral proceedings to better ensure transparency.
“Panawagan ko nga vigilance is not enough. Panawagan ko sa kanila baka pwede na sila mag-resort sa shaming para pwedeng tablan ng hiya ang iba,” he said.
(I told the groups that vigilance is not enough and that they should resort to shaming against lawmakers who sneak in questionable realignments.)
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed budget.

Ejercito also confirmed that the bicameral deliberations which would reconcile the Senate and the House of Representatives’ differing versions of the budget bill, would also be livestreamed to allow the public to watch the proceedings in real time.
Lacson also raised concerns over the questionable coordinates in the proposed 2027 national budget flagged by budget advocacy groups.

“Akala ko malayo na ‘yung Leyte, hanggang sa marinig ko yung People’s Budget Coalition, umabot pa ng Celebes Sea. So hindi ito typo error kasi naka-geotag, dapat pinpointed talaga. Yun ang gamit nga ng geotagging, na kung saan madaling hanapin yung project at madaling ma-inspect para pag yung quality control nila, madaling malaman kung talaga nagawa yung proyekto,” the senator said.

(I thought Leyte was already far enough, until the People’s Budget Coalition flagged a project whose coordinates pointed to the Celebes Sea. So this is not a mere typo error because the projects are geotagged and should be pinpointed. That’s what geotagging is for– to make it easy to locate and inspect a project so its quality can be checked and verified.)

Meanwhile, Lacson said senators would relay Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Giovanni Lopez’s requirements for project funding, including program of works, feasibility studies, and geotagging.
The senator also said the Unified Account Code Structure (UACS) throughout the process to ensure smooth tracking of project implementation.

articles.title: Pope Leo accepts resignation Bangued bishop
articles.summary: The Pontiff accepted Jaucian’s resignation on Sunday, November 8, according to the Vatican Press Office.

blocks.text: November 8, 2026 | 2:49pm
Bangued, Abra Bishop Leopoldo Jaucian
Diocese of Cubao
MANILA, Philippines — Pope Leo XIV has accepted the resignation of the Diocese of Bangued, Abra, Bishop Leopoldo Jaucian.
The Pontiff accepted Jaucian’s resignation on Sunday, November 8, according to the Vatican Press Office.
Jaucian, 66, is a priest from the Society of Divine Word (SVD), has served as the bishop of Bangued since 2007, upon the appointment of Pope Benedict XVI.
He replaced the former Bishop Artemio Lomboy Rillera, who was also from the SVD.
Catholic Bishops are required to submit their resignation upon reaching the age of 75, according to church law.

According to CBCP News, the Pontiff accepted his resignation under Paragraph 2 of Canon 401 of the Code of Canon Law, which provides for bishops who are unable to fulfill their duties because of ill health or another grave reason.
Jaucian was ordained to the priesthood in 1988 at the Divine Word College Chapel in Urdaneta City.
With Jaucian’s resignation, the CBCP News said the number of vacant ecclesiastical jurisdictions in the Philippines has risen to seven.
These include the dioceses of Bangued, Parañaque, Masbate, Kabankalan, Ilagan and Borongan, as well as the Apostolic Vicariate of Jolo.
With Jaucian's resignation, an apostolic administrator is expected to be appointed within eight days the prelate's resignation.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Who are qualified to get DepEd's new laptops for teachers?
articles.summary: The Department of Education released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:31pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) released the guidelines on who are eligible to receive the brand new laptops it procured for public school teachers.
The DepEd earlier secured over 172,000 units of Apple's MacBook Neo laptops, which the tech giant reportedly acknowledged as its "biggest education deal ever" for its MacBook line.

"Dahil limitado pa ang available units na kayang mabili sa allocated national budget, hindi pa lahat ng guro ay mabibigyan sa round na ito. Sisikapin nating matiyak ang patas at maayos na pamamahagi ng mga laptop," said DepEd.
Who are eligible for the budget MacBook laptops?
DepEd said that it would prioritize schools and teachers who have yet to receive any laptop.
It would also prioritize those personnel holding EdTech leadership roles or those actively helping in teaching with technology.
The beneficiaries should be active employees in the listed school during the selection, it added.
Teachers who still have a working government/school laptop issued last January 2023 to November 6, 2026 are not eligible to receive the brand new units.
However, DepEd said that those who bought their own laptops are not disqualified from receiving MacBook Neo units.

Further, the department said that former laptop recipients can still receive the MacBook Neo units by providing official records declaring that their laptops are unserviceable and decommissioned; lost or damaged because of calamity; or lost due to theft or robbery.
The department said that eligible teachers should have an active DepEd email account and the two-factor authentication must be on.
How will the recipients be chosen?
According to DepEd, there will be a draw if the allotted units are not enough for the priority groups.

Moreover, DepEd reminded that the brand new laptops are government properties. Hence, they cannot be sold or transferred to new owners without the proper authorization by the school head and property custodian.
If a teacher will be transferred to another school, the department said the laptop accountability shall be transferred as well to the new school.
Once a teacher decides to retire or resign, the laptop shall be returned to the supply officer or property custodian.
Each MacBook Neo unit was procured at P43,000, which is P6,900 below the current suggested retail price in the Philippines for the base model.
The DepEd said this included a five-year warranty, which is a first for the agency's laptop procurement, instead of the typical one-year warranty. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm
articles.summary:
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo

The Prince of Wales’s
articles.byline: Rebecca Ratcliffe, Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça

blocks.text: The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.

A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.

Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.

Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.

This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.

Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.

Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.

“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.

A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
after newsletter promotion

Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.

“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.

Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”

Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.

The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.

“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

articles.title: Does Andy Burnham’s pivot from press to social media put scrutiny at risk?
articles.summary:
A lifestyle podcast or brief TV clip is less taxing than a full press conference – but No 10 insists the PM is not ducking accountability

In an interview this week Andy Burnham said he…

blocks.text: In an interview this week Andy Burnham said he believed the traditional media was less relevant and the world was “not like that any more”. But some people are now asking: does this change in approach mean less scrutiny?

The question was in part prompted by Burnham’s decision to travel to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) without the usual accompanying pack of reporters, instead bringing just one TV crew and a news agency journalist.

Across three days of the event, which featured discussions of an apology for slavery and possible reparations, and during which significant global events occurred, including the US midterm elections, Burnham faced just seven-and-a-half minutes of media questions, via two brief BBC chats.
Downing Street officials say Chogm is unique in offering very limited access to journalists, and that the prime minister had done other interviews and media events beforehand.

But it was nonetheless a change. At the last Commonwealth summit in 2024, Keir Starmer took along a full press contingent, submitting himself to both a press conference and a “huddle” – an off-camera but on-record Q&A on the government plane on the way over, in which each travelling journalist gets a question.

When it comes to communications, Burnham and his team are unapologetic about doing things differently. As well as talking to influencers and podcasters, the prime minister is an adept social media performer himself, with an output that ranges from more traditional pieces to camera to a YouTube video where he and the chancellor, John Healey, ranked pub snacks.

blocks.caption: In a video on Andy Burnham’s TikTok account, he went for a run with Mo Farah.  Photograph: Andy Burnham/TikTok

blocks.text: Asked about the pub snack video in an interview with ITV that was broadcast this week, Burnham said he hoped such content “connects with people, particularly younger people who may have felt quite distanced from politics”.

Asked whether his focus on that sort of output was a sign he cared less about rightwing newspapers such as the Sun and the Daily Mail said about him, Burnham replied: “Definitely. I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there, and the whole world is meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that any more.”

While no one in politics disagrees with the need for leaders to keep up with the fast-changing ways in which people consume news, it is undeniable that an interview on a lifestyle podcast, or a brief TV clip in which the reporter has to cover all the news of the day, is less taxing than a full press conference with specialist journalists.

No 10 is insistent that Burnham does not dodge scrutiny, pointing to recent longer-form interviews, as well as a grilling last month on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, where the comfy sofas generally come with robust questioning.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham being interviewed during the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing Street

blocks.text: Some observers nonetheless detect what they see as efforts by his team to make Burnham’s mix of media engagements slightly less onerous than it might be.

“When the going is good, he can probably get away with it,” said one former media adviser who worked with several Conservative prime ministers. “But if things get worse and it feels like the press is getting shut out, or not being given the chance to properly scrutinise policies, then in my experience the media are pretty good at working as a pack, and will come down quite hard.”
after newsletter promotion

There is a particular incentive for a prime minister to dodge the traditional on-plane media huddle en route to a summit, which can often involve more than a dozen questions, ranging from global events to relative trivia.

The repercussions can be significant, usually more so for prime ministers already under pressure. In a passing remark on a flight to China in 2018, Theresa May said she planned to fight the next election, galvanising critics on her own backbenches.
“Misadventures have a way of happening when prime ministers go out on the road,” said Paul Harrison, who was May’s press secretary.

“A huddle with the travelling press pack is about as unpredictable a high-wire act as there is for a PM – potentially 15 journalists each asking blind questions on absolutely anything they like. And a bad answer delivered en route to a summit can still be making headlines long after you’ve got home.”

Liz Jarvis, a Liberal Democrat MP who is a former journalist and sits on the culture, media and sport select committee, said while it was undeniable that politicians needed to communicate differently, it felt as though Burnham was being shielded at times.

She said: “He is a very skilled orator, but when you break down his PMQs answers, for example, there sometimes isn’t much substance to it. When the honeymoon period ends he will be held to account, so he can’t avoid media scrutiny for ever.”

articles.title: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?
articles.summary: Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

image.caption: Finding a path away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will once again be on the agenda at COP this yearImage: Goksel Yapar/AFP

blocks.text: With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.
Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.
Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry?

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.
Climate talks not enough to save
Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.
"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."
Climate 'clubs' banding together to enact change

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to come to an agreement, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.
"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."
Small states push fossil fuel treaty amid Iran energy crisis
An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.
Spark new momentum on decarbonization

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.
Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."
It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.
Climate financing 'far from what's needed'

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

blocks.caption: Island nations and coastal communities in places like Panama (above) are at risk of rising seasImage: Martin Bernetti/AFP

blocks.text: But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.
The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.
"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power, on which Germany and other industrialized nations rely to shape policy to fight climate change.
Concrete action would make COP31 a success
Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.
Kenya's young climate influencers driving real change
For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.
When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.
This article was originally written in German.
